title: Kernel Panic
genre: 1976 hard rock with an early punk edge
description: Kernel Panic is the 1976 third album from Procedural Byts: twelve fast, raw tracks of hard rock with an early punk edge about the program that runs all the other programs. Nyble sings lead and plays bass, Byt plays lead guitar, and Bytes plays drums and sings backup. Booting, system calls, processes and fork, scheduling, context switches, locks, deadlock, virtual memory, page faults, file systems, device drivers and the crash that takes everything down. The recording sessions deadlocked for three weeks until someone moved the duck. Play loud. Then reboot.
tagline: The 1976 hard-rock-meets-punk album from Procedural Byts: an operating systems course in twelve fast songs, from boot to kernel panic.
lineup: Still a power trio. Nyble sings lead on every song and plays bass guitar. Byt plays lead guitar. Bytes plays drums and sings backup.

members.name: Nyble
members.bio: Four bits and the band’s scheduler, whether anyone asked her to be or not. Nyble sings lead on every song, plays bass, and on this album she also had to reap a zombie.

members.name: Byt
members.bio: One bit, and the only member who has ever tried to fork himself. Byt plays lead guitar and most of the solos, which on this record include two solos at once, a solo that asks permission, and a solo that only pretends to use the whole neck.

members.name: Bytes
members.bio: Eight bits, eight flip-flops, and the person holding the drumsticks during the deadlock. Bytes plays drums, sings backup, and is the one who finally breaks the deadlock in the middle of the song, with a single crash cymbal.

members.name: Null
members.bio: Sat on the only lyric sheet for three weeks. Resolved the deadlock by being moved. Has not commented.

story.heading: The Deadlock Sessions
paragraphs: By 1976 the band had played enough shows to have strong opinions about who should go first, who should wait, and who was hogging the microphone. So they wrote an album about the program that settles those arguments for every computer: the operating system.

The studio had one good microphone, one good amplifier and one good pair of drumsticks. Within a week, Nyble had the microphone and was waiting for Byt to finish his guitar part, Byt had the amp and was waiting for Bytes to finish the drums, and Bytes had the sticks and was waiting for Nyble’s lyrics. Nobody moved for three weeks.

The deadlock ended when the producer picked up Null, who had been sitting on the only copy of the lyric sheet the whole time, and everyone realized they could start again. Deadlock (Nobody Moves) was written that afternoon.
After that, the producer ran the sessions round robin: four hours each, then out, ready or not. Byt complained that he was being starved. Bytes pointed out that the real problem was the zombie.

The zombie was Byt’s fault. He had tried to fork himself so he could play rhythm and lead at the same time. The child process hung around the studio for days, eating everyone’s sandwiches, until Nyble finally reaped it.
On the last day, the tape machine crashed hard. The band recorded the title track in one take while it rebooted, which is why the album ends the way it does.

cover_sub: The third album, 1976. Twelve fast songs about the program that runs all the others.

songs.title: Bootstrap

parts.label: Intro (spoken)
lines: Power on.

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: Press the switch and the lights come on,
Firmware wakes and the dark is gone.
A tiny loader in the ROM so small
Loads a bigger loader, and that loads it all!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Bootstrap! Pull yourself up!
Bootstrap! Fill the empty cup!
From a single spark to the kernel’s crown,
Bootstrap, bootstrap, you can’t keep it down!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: The kernel’s loaded and it takes the throne,
Counts up the memory and claims it as its own,
Starts the first process, the father of them all,
Then the login prompt waits for your call!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Chicken or the egg? (The loader!)
Who loads the loader? (The ROM!)

parts.label: Instrumental break: full band
parts.desc: Bytes starts with a single kick drum, the firmware. Nyble’s bass comes in on top, the bootloader. Then Byt’s guitar crashes in, the kernel, and the whole system is up.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Bootstrap! Pull yourself up!
Bootstrap! Fill the empty cup!
From a single spark to the kernel’s crown,
Bootstrap, bootstrap, you can’t keep it down!

songs.note: Each instrument starts the next, the way each stage of a boot loads the one after it.
songs.lesson: Booting: firmware in read-only memory runs a tiny bootloader, which loads the operating system kernel. The kernel sets up memory and hardware, starts the first process, and the system comes up ready for you to log in. The name comes from “pulling yourself up by your bootstraps.”

songs.title: System Call

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: I’m just a program in user mode,
Fenced in my box on a narrow road.
I can’t touch the disk and I can’t touch the wire,
Only the kernel gets to play with the fire!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: System call! Knock on the kernel’s door!
System call! Ask for something more!
Read it, write it, open it, make it so,
Cross into kernel mode and back you go!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: The trap goes off and the mode flips around,
The kernel checks you out before you hit the ground.
Are you allowed? Is the request okay?
It does the job and sends you on your way!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Protection! (Protection!) Keep the programs apart!
One bad program can’t break everybody’s heart!

parts.label: Lead guitar solo: Byt
parts.desc: Byt plays quiet, muted riffs: user mode. To play a loud note, he has to raise his hand to Nyble, who stomps on his distortion pedal for one phrase, kernel mode, then switches it off again.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: System call! Knock on the kernel’s door!
System call! Ask for something more!
Read it, write it, open it, make it so,
Cross into kernel mode and back you go!

songs.note: Byt had to ask permission before every loud note. It was the longest he had ever gone without breaking anything.
songs.lesson: Programs run in user mode with limited privileges, and the kernel runs in kernel mode with full access to the hardware. A system call (like read, write, open or fork) traps into the kernel, which checks the request, does the privileged work and returns. This protection stops one program from crashing or spying on the others.

songs.title: Fork in the Road

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: A program on the disk is just a list of things to do,
A process is the program running, living, breathing through.
It’s got its own memory, its own counter and its stack,
A number for its name, the PID upon its back!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Fork in the road! (One becomes two!)
Fork in the road! (The child looks just like you!)
The parent goes one way, the child goes the other,
Fork in the road, and they don’t know each other!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Fork gives a zero to the child, the parent gets its name,
Exec wipes the child clean and gives it a brand-new game.
The parent waits for the child to finish and to die,
Or the child becomes a zombie, and you’ll never say goodbye!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Zombie! (Zombie!) Dead but in the table!
Reap it with a wait, if you’re able!

parts.label: Twin solo: Byt and Nyble
parts.desc: Byt plays a phrase, and at the fork Nyble’s bass copies it note for note. Then the two lines split and go their own ways, until Byt stops and waits for Nyble to finish before the last chorus.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Fork in the road! (One becomes two!)
Fork in the road! (The child looks just like you!)
The parent goes one way, the child goes the other,
Fork in the road, and they don’t know each other!

songs.note: Byt tried to fork himself during the sessions to play two parts at once. The child process hung around the studio for days eating sandwiches until Nyble reaped it.
songs.lesson: A process is a running program with its own memory, registers, stack and process ID. In Unix, `fork()` copies the process (it returns 0 to the child and the child’s ID to the parent), `exec()` replaces the child’s program with a new one, and `wait()` lets the parent collect the child when it finishes. A finished child nobody waits for becomes a zombie.

songs.title: Round Robin

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: Ten programs and a single CPU,
Who goes first, and how long till you’re through?
The scheduler picks and the scheduler decides
Who gets to run and who waits outside!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Round robin! (Take your turn!)
Round robin! (Watch the time slice burn!)
Run a little while, then the back of the line,
Round and round, everybody gets their time!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: First come, first served, and the long one blocks the way,
Shortest job first, but the long ones never play.
Priority runs the important ones fast,
But starve the little guys and they’ll never get past!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Time’s up! (Time’s up!) The timer says so!
Preempt the process and let the next one go!

parts.label: Trading solo: whole band
parts.desc: Byt, Nyble and Bytes take turns with exactly four bars each, three times around. When your time slice ends you stop, even mid-phrase, and the next player goes.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Round robin! (Take your turn!)
Round robin! (Watch the time slice burn!)
Run a little while, then the back of the line,
Round and round, everybody gets their time!

songs.note: Each member gets exactly four bars of the solo and then gets cut off, ready or not.
songs.lesson: The scheduler decides which process gets the CPU. First come, first served is simple, but long jobs block short ones. Shortest job first cuts waiting but can starve long jobs, and priority scheduling can starve low priorities. Round robin gives every process a time slice and uses a timer interrupt to switch to the next.

songs.title: Context Switch

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: Running process A when the timer goes off,
Freeze it in the moment, take its registers off.
Save it in the table, every value in its place,
Load up process B and put on its face!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Context switch! Change the scene!
Context switch! Save the machine!
Freeze one, wake one, nobody can tell,
Context switch, and they all think it’s going well!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Every switch has a cost, a little time that’s gone,
Saving and restoring while nobody’s getting on.
Switch too often and the work begins to slow,
Too seldom and the waiting starts to grow!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Process control block! (Who you are!)
Counter, stack, registers! (Where you are!)

parts.label: Lead guitar solo: Byt
parts.desc: Byt plays two completely different solos, switching between them every few bars. Each time, he freezes one mid-phrase and later picks it up at exactly the same note, with a tiny gap at every switch.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Context switch! Change the scene!
Context switch! Save the machine!
Freeze one, wake one, nobody can tell,
Context switch, and they all think it’s going well!

songs.note: The hardest song on the album to play live. Byt has to keep two solos in his head at once.
songs.lesson: A context switch saves the running process’s state (registers, program counter, stack pointer) in its process control block and restores another process’s state. That’s how one CPU looks like it’s running many programs at once. Every switch costs time, so time slices balance responsiveness against overhead.

songs.title: Lock It Down

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: Two programs reach for the same number at the same time,
Both of them read it, both add one, and only one makes the line.
The total should be two, but it’s only one again,
The critical section needs a guard at the gate, my friend!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Lock it down! (Only one inside!)
Lock it down! (The rest wait outside!)
Grab the lock, do the work, then let it go,
Mutual exclusion, one at a time, you know!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: A semaphore counts how many can get through,
A mutex is a key, and there’s only one for you.
Forget to unlock and the others wait for good,
Lock too much and nothing moves the way it should!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Race condition! (Who got there first?)
Lock the critical section, or the data’s cursed!

parts.label: Bass solo: Nyble
parts.desc: Only one instrument may hold the melody at a time. Nyble holds it, hands it to Byt, then takes it back. Once, they both grab it at the same time, and the clash is so ugly they never do it again.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Lock it down! (Only one inside!)
Lock it down! (The rest wait outside!)
Grab the lock, do the work, then let it go,
Mutual exclusion, one at a time, you know!

songs.note: The studio had one good microphone. This song is about that microphone.
songs.lesson: When processes or threads share data, a race condition can corrupt it: two increments can turn into one. The code that touches shared data is a critical section. A mutex (a lock) lets only one in at a time, and a semaphore counts how many can enter. Always release your locks, and lock only what you need.

songs.title: Deadlock (Nobody Moves)

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: I’ve got the drumsticks and I’m waiting for the mic,
You’ve got the mic, you’re waiting on the bass you like,
She’s got the bass and she’s waiting for the sticks,
Nobody gives, and nobody’s gonna fix!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Deadlock! (Nobody moves!)
Deadlock! (Nobody grooves!)
Everybody holding on and everybody stuck,
Waiting in a circle, deadlock, no luck!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: It takes four things together to freeze the whole band:
One at a time, and holding on while you wait to land,
No one can take it from you, and the waiting forms a ring,
Break just one of the four and the band can sing!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Five philosophers at dinner, five forks on the table,
Everybody grabs the left one, and nobody’s able!

parts.label: Deadlock break: full band
parts.desc: The band holds one chord, each waiting for someone else. Then four full bars of silence. Then Bytes smashes a crash cymbal, takes the riff away from everyone, and the song starts moving again.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Deadlock! (Nobody moves!)
Deadlock! (Nobody grooves!)
Everybody holding on and everybody stuck,
Waiting in a circle, deadlock, no luck!

songs.note: The recording sessions deadlocked for three weeks. This song is how they got out.
songs.lesson: Deadlock happens when processes each hold a resource while waiting for one another in a cycle. It needs four conditions at once: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait. Break any one, for example by always taking resources in the same order, and deadlock can’t happen. The dining philosophers are the classic example.

songs.title: Virtual Memory

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: Every program thinks it owns the whole machine,
Every address from zero to the top it’s ever seen.
But it’s an illusion, a map inside the dark,
The real memory’s smaller, and it’s shared by every spark!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Virtual memory! A world that isn’t there!
Virtual memory! Addresses in the air!
Every process gets its own and none of them collide,
The page table knows where the real ones hide!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Split it into pages, cut the frames to size,
The table maps the virtual to the real, a clean disguise.
One program can’t touch another, they live in separate rooms,
And the pages you’re not using sleep down in the tombs!

parts.label: Bridge

songs.title: Page Fault

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: I reach for a page, but the page isn’t there,
It’s out on the disk, down the hall, down the stair.
The hardware cries fault and the kernel steps in,
Fetches it back, and we try it again!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Page fault! (Not in memory!)
Page fault! (Go and get it for me!)
Kick one out to make some room,
Page fault, page fault, impending doom!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Who gets evicted when the memory’s full?
The least recently used is the one you should pull.
But too many programs and too little space,
And you’re swapping all day, and you’re thrashing the place!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Thrashing! (Thrashing!) Nothing gets done!
All of the time swapping, and no one has fun!

parts.label: Drum solo: Bytes
parts.desc: Bytes plays a steady beat, but every so often he reaches for a drum that isn’t in his kit and has to stop while a roadie runs to fetch it and carries another one away. By the end the roadie is swapping drums faster than Bytes can play them: thrashing.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Page fault! (Not in memory!)
Page fault! (Go and get it for me!)
Kick one out to make some room,
Page fault, page fault, impending doom!

songs.note: Bytes’s drum kit was split between the studio and a storage room down the hall. The roadie ran a lot.
songs.lesson: When a process touches a page that isn’t in physical memory, a page fault happens: the OS loads the page from disk, evicting another if memory is full, using a replacement policy like least recently used (LRU). When there isn’t enough memory for what the programs are actively using, the system thrashes, spending its time swapping instead of working.

songs.title: Everything Is a File

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: Names in a directory, folders in a tree,
Start up at the root and follow the path to me.
Slash, home, Nyble, songs, that’s the way that you go,
Every file has a name and a place, you know!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Everything is a file! (Everything is a file!)
The disk, the printer, the keyboard all the while!
Open it, read it, write it, close it tight,
Everything is a file, and the file is right!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Behind the name, an inode holds the key,
Where the blocks are scattered and how big it’ll be.
Read, write, execute, the permissions on the door,
Owner, group and others, who can see what for!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Read! (Read!) Write! (Write!) Execute! (Execute!)
Check the permissions before you touch the loot!

parts.label: Bass solo: Nyble
parts.desc: Nyble’s solo is a directory tree: one root phrase, and each new phrase opens a folder inside the last. At the bottom she finds the file she was looking for, then climbs back up the same path to the root.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Everything is a file! (Everything is a file!)
The disk, the printer, the keyboard all the while!
Open it, read it, write it, close it tight,
Everything is a file, and the file is right!

songs.note: The only song where all three members sing the whole chorus together.
songs.lesson: A file system organizes data into files and nested directories starting from a root, named by paths. Metadata (in Unix, an inode) records where a file’s blocks are, its size and its permissions: read, write and execute for the owner, the group and everyone else. Unix even treats devices as files, so one open/read/write/close interface works for everything.

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: Every printer speaks a language of its own,
Every disk has its secrets, every terminal its tone.

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Device driver! Talk to the machine!
Device driver! Speak to the unseen!
One interface on top and a thousand down below,
Device driver, driver, make the hardware go!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Buffer it and queue it, because the disk is slow,
Gather up the writes and then let them flow.

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Abstraction! (One for all!)
The driver hides the hardware behind the wall!

parts.label: Lead guitar solo: Byt
parts.desc: Byt plays the same riff through three different amplifiers, one after another, and Nyble adjusts the knobs on each so they all come out sounding identical. The driver hides the difference.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Device driver! Talk to the machine!
Device driver! Speak to the unseen!
One interface on top and a thousand down below,
Device driver, driver, make the hardware go!

songs.note: Recorded through three different amplifiers. You shouldn’t be able to tell.
songs.lesson: A device driver is kernel code that knows how to control one kind of hardware and offers the rest of the operating system a standard interface, so nothing else needs to know the details. Drivers handle buffering, queuing requests and responding to the device’s interrupts.

songs.title: Kernel Panic

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: A pointer to nowhere, deep inside the core,
The kernel trips and stumbles and it hits the floor.
There’s no one above it to catch it when it falls,
When the kernel breaks, it’s the end of it all!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Kernel panic! Everything stops!
Kernel panic! The whole system drops!
No safety net, no handler, no one left to call,
Kernel panic, panic, it takes down them all!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: A program crashes and the kernel cleans it up,
But who cleans up the kernel when it drinks the poisoned cup?
Dump the memory, print the message on the screen,
Then reboot and start again, the cleanest you’ve ever seen!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Panic! (Panic!) Halt and dump the core!
Reboot! (Reboot!) Start it like before!

parts.label: Crash and reboot: full band
parts.desc: Everything goes wrong at once: the band plays every part at full speed into a wall of noise and stops dead. Silence. Then the opening riff of Bootstrap, from the top. Reboot.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Kernel panic! Everything stops!
Kernel panic! The whole system drops!
No safety net, no handler, no one left to call,
Kernel panic, panic, it takes down them all!

songs.note: The tape machine crashed on the last day. The band recorded this in one take while it rebooted.
songs.lesson: A kernel panic is a fatal error inside the operating system kernel itself. Nothing runs above the kernel to recover it, so it halts, often saving a memory dump for debugging, and the machine has to reboot. That’s why kernel code has to be especially careful: a bug there takes everything down.
